#### `s20-round1`

**Wren**: Yes, commander! On it, commander!  
_Every time you point at Wren, she salutes and says something. You point at her rather a lot._  
**Wren**: Yes, commander. Yes, commander. Commander, that’s nine times. I’m only little.  
**Pixel**: Notice: your sticks are low. Sticks are scarce now. Notice: you can’t recruit more children. You’ve run out of mittens.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity: choosing when there isn’t enough  
> **Pixel**: Your sticks are scarce. You can’t get any more. What’s the smart thing to do?  
> - ✅ Save them for the most important job, and build the rest from snow. → Correct. When there isn’t enough of something, you have to choose what it’s for. That’s called scarcity. Everybody deals with it. Shops, towns, and forts.
> - Use them all on the first thing you see. → Then there are none left for the thing that matters. When something is scarce, choose carefully what it’s for. Save sticks for the most important job.
> - Cry into your mittens. → You’ve run out of mittens. A better plan: when something is scarce, save it for the most important job and use snow for the rest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that scarcity (not having enough) means choosing what to use something for._

**Pixel**: Ruling: a snowball that hits a snowman is friendly fire. The snowman has feelings. He’s called Derek.  
_At the whistle, your wall is knee-high, fat and lumpy. Theirs is shoulder-high, thin, and has battlements._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): comparing two designs: why a wide base is steadier  
> _Compare the walls. Yours: low, fat and lumpy. Theirs: tall and thin. Which one is harder to knock over?_  
> - ✅ Mine: low and wide. → Yes. A wide base and a low height make things steady. That’s why pyramids are wide at the bottom, and why a tall, thin wall wobbles.
> - Theirs: tall and thin. → It looks grander! But tall and thin is wobbly: one good push and it tips. A low, wide wall is steadier. Remember that.
> - They’re exactly the same. → Same snow, different shapes! The low, wide one is steadier. Shape matters as much as stuff.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two wall designs and learned that a wide base and low height make a structure steadier._

**Tilly**: Economy! I put everyone on snow from the very start. I learned it off the Tax Toad.  
**Pixel**: Round one: a draw. Theirs is taller. Yours is fatter. Ruling: both of them are walls.

#### `s20-intel`

_Zip comes back with snow on his eyebrows and something urgent to say, which he says by running round you nine times._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step take-away problem  
> _Zip’s tracks say: their fort started with 10 children. 3 went home. 4 more are busy patting the wall._  
> _How many are left to defend it?_  
> - 7 → That’s after the 3 went home: 10 − 3 = 7. But 4 more are busy with the wall. 7 − 4 = 3.
> - ✅ 3 → Yes! Two steps: 10 − 3 = 7, then 7 − 4 = 3. Three defenders. “Almost nobody” is right.
> - 6 → Let’s do it in two steps. 10 − 3 = 7 still there… then 7 − 4 = 3 left. Three defenders.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step subtraction problem (10 − 3 − 4 = 3)._

**Pixel**: Ruling: children are not bricks.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fair play: using a chance or waiting (think question)  
> _Their fort is thin right now. Is it fair to attack while three of them are missing?_  
> - Yes. In a game, you use your chances. → That’s a fair answer. Lots of games reward spotting a chance. The other commander would probably do the same, only louder.
> - No. A fair fight means both sides are ready. → That’s a fair answer too. Footballers often kick the ball out when someone on the other team is hurt. It isn’t a rule. It’s fair play.
> - It depends on what everyone agreed. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Fairness often comes down to the rules everyone agreed before the game. Pixel’s forty-one pages don’t say.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed up whether it is fair to take advantage of the other side’s bad luck in a game._

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-1, notice): what a blizzard is  
> _A blizzard is a snowstorm with very strong wind that goes on for a long time._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): putting safety before winning  
> _Everyone is scared and the game has stopped. What matters most now?_  
> - ✅ Getting every child, from both forts, somewhere safe. → Yes. When something real goes wrong, the game stops and people come first. All of them, whichever fort they’re from.
> - Grabbing the flag. We were one dash away! → It’s tempting! But a game can wait. People can’t. The most important thing is getting every child safe.
> - Finding just your own fort. → Your fort matters. But so does the small crying person, whoever they belong to. In a real emergency, everyone counts.
> _For grown-ups: Decided that keeping everyone safe matters more than winning a game._

**Tilly**: Is this a trick? Is this a strategy?  
**You**: Yes.  
_A strategy is just a plan for getting what you want. Right now, what you want is everybody warm._  

**Choices**

- **Kick open your wall and shout them all in.**
    - You kick a gap in your own wall. “IN! EVERYONE IN!”
    - Your fort has been taught all morning to do what you say. It does it, and starts pulling the others in by their scarves.
- **Carry your wall to them, snowball by snowball.**
    - Your gatherers know how to move snow fast. You taught them that this morning.
    - It turns out that was what it was for.
- **Meet in the middle. Both walls, one shelter.**
    - You meet in the ditch between the forts. Both sides bring snow. Both sides bring sticks.
    - The catapult becomes a roof beam. Derek the snowman becomes a door.

#### `s20-count`

**Pixel**: Head count.  
**Pixel**: …Everyone. Even Gordon.  
**Gordon**: I got hit by a whole sky.  
_Inside it is close and blue and smells of wet wool. Forty mittens steam. Somebody is eating snow. Pixel rules against it, then allows it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division as sharing into pairs  
> _Forty mittens are steaming. Every child has two. How many children are in the shelter?_  
> - ✅ 20 → Yes! 40 ÷ 2 = 20. Twenty children, and not one mitten missing. Ruling: that is everyone.
> - 40 → That’s the mittens! Each child has two, so share the 40 into pairs. 40 ÷ 2 = 20 children.
> - 10 → That would be if each child had four mittens. Two each: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 children.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 40 mittens into pairs to find 20 children (40 ÷ 2 = 20)._

**Tilly**: That’s my wall, in our roof. That bit’s mine.  
_The roof is sticks from both forts, leaning together in pointed pairs, with snow packed on top._  

> **Lesson** (science, do): why triangles make strong frames  
> **Pixel**: Look up. Two sticks leaning together, with the ground underneath, make a triangle.  
> **Pixel**: Push on a triangle and it keeps its shape. Push on a square and it squashes into a diamond.  
> **Pixel**: That’s why roofs and bridges are full of triangles.  
> **Pixel**: Tap every triangle you can find in the roof.  
> Check: `edu:tap:shape:triangle:roof`
> _For grown-ups: Found triangles in a roof frame and learned that triangles keep their shape under pressure, which makes frames strong._

**Wren**: Commander? Which fort won?  
_Outside, the wind drops as suddenly as it came. Somebody pokes a hole in the roof to look._  

#### `s20-complete`

_The sky is clear and black and enormous. Every star the valley owns is out, and a few it has borrowed._  
_Nobody goes home. Both forts lie on their backs in one fort and look up._  
**Wren**: That one’s a mitten. That one’s Gordon. That one’s Derek.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): why the stars show on a clear night, and constellations  
> _Why can you see so many stars tonight?_  
> - ✅ The clouds have gone, and it’s properly dark. → Yes. The blizzard’s clouds have blown away, so nothing hides the stars. Long ago, people joined stars into pictures too, called constellations. Wren has just invented the Mitten.
> - The blizzard blew new stars in. → Ha! The stars were there all along. The blizzard’s clouds were hiding them. Now the clouds have gone, you can see them all.
> - Stars only come out in winter. → Stars are there all year, even in the daytime. The Sun is just so bright that it hides them. Tonight it’s dark and clear.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars are always in the sky but are hidden by clouds and by daylight; met the word constellation._

**Pixel**: Final ruling. Both forts win. I’ve written it in pen. Pen is final.  
**Tilly**: So what was it for, then? The economy and the scouting and the counters?  
**You**: So we could build one fort fast, when it mattered.  
**Tilly**: …That’s annoying. That’s a really good answer.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme of a story  
> _A theme is the big idea a story is about. What do you think this story’s theme is?_  
> - ✅ Skills and plans matter most when they help everybody. → Yes. Gathering, scouting and teamwork were practice for a war. In the end they built a shelter for both sides.
> - Always win, whatever happens. → Nobody won! Or everybody did. The big idea is that the skills mattered most when they helped everyone.
> - Snow is cold. → True, and Gordon would agree. But the big idea is bigger: plans and skills matter most when they help everybody.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of a story: skills and plans matter most when used to help everyone._

_Up at the cottage a lamp is lit in the window, and somebody in a blanket is watching the Common._  
_Tilly puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles the supper call, rising at the end. From the window, faintly, it comes back._  
**Tilly**: She can still do it.  
**Pixel**: Prizes. Commander’s hat: it was a tea cosy. Snowball launcher: a prototype. Ruling: point it away from Gordon.  
**Pixel**: And the fort’s yours. I’ll build you one for the Grove that only comes out when it snows.  
_All morning you practised winning. In the end, the useful part was building something big enough for everybody._  

### Glossary

- **referee**: The person who makes sure everyone follows the rules of a game.
- **economy**: How people get, share and use the things they need.
- **scarce**: In short supply, so there isn’t enough for everything.
- **battlements**: The up-and-down gaps along the top of a castle wall.
- **scout**: Someone sent ahead to look around and bring back information.
- **magnificent**: Very grand and impressive.
- **strategy**: A plan for how to win or reach a goal.
- **blizzard**: A snowstorm with very strong wind that lasts a long time.
- **constellation**: A group of stars that people join up into a picture.

## S21. CL-4NK

- `s21-step1`: Show Clank round the Grove. · _He follows you on one wheel. Go round things, not over them. He can’t do steps, kerbs or roots, though he believes he can._
- `s21-step2`: Undo Clank’s helping before he helps anything else. · _Dry the cat, prop up the tree, then try to catch Clank before he reaches the step. In that order, if you can. You won’t._
- `s21-step3`: Find Clank. · _Follow the wheel-track through the thyme. He’s hiding somewhere he thinks he fits in._
- `s21-step4`: Help Byte build a ramp for the cottage step. · _Byte measures; you saw. Measure twice. Byte will measure eleven times. Let him._
- `s21-step5`: Stay in the Grove with Clank until dusk. · _Feed the Nubbins first. Then sit by the cottage step and do nothing at all. It’s harder than it sounds._

#### `s21-unveil`

_Something is coming up the lane, squeaking. It’s Pixel, pushing a wheelbarrow with a tea towel over it._  
**Pixel**: Morning. Don’t be alarmed. Be a bit alarmed. A normal amount.  
**Pixel**: After Sparks fixed the lantern posts, there was a whole box of parts left over. I couldn’t just leave them in a box.  
_Off comes the tea towel. Underneath: a lantern hood, a glass chimney, a brass wick-winder for a nose, and one wheel._  
**Pixel**: Garden helper. Watering, weeding, carrying. In theory.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what a robot is  
> **Pixel**: A robot is a machine that can sense things, follow instructions, and move or do jobs.  
> **Pixel**: The instructions are called a program. People write them. I wrote his. Mostly in capital letters, it turns out.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a robot is a machine that senses, follows a program of instructions written by people, and acts._

_Pixel turns the wick-winder. Something inside warms up, then whistles, rising, like a kettle that has just heard good news._  
**Clank**: HELLO! Hello hello HELLO. I am CL-4NK! The four is silent! So is the dash!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): numbers standing in for letters in a name  
> _Clank says the four in CL-4NK is silent. But look at its shape. Which letter is the 4 pretending to be?_  
> - ✅ A → Yes! CL-A-NK. A 4 looks a bit like a pointy A. People sometimes swap in numbers that look like letters. So the four isn’t silent at all. It’s an A in disguise. Don’t tell him.
> - B → B would make CL-B-NK, which sounds like a sneeze. A 4 looks more like a pointy A: CL-A-NK. Clank!
> - F → CL-F-NK? Tricky to say! The 4 is shaped a bit like a pointy A: CL-A-NK. Clank!
> _For grown-ups: Decoded a name where a number (4) stands in for a similar-looking letter (A)._

**Clank**: Call me Clank! You are my BEST FRIEND!  
**You**: We’ve only just—  
**Clank**: Best friend. Decided. Announcement: I HAVE A BEST FRIEND!  
_He rolls forward to shake your hand, rolls straight off the cottage step, and lands on his hood in the thyme._  
**Clank**: Announcement! I have found the step!  
**Clank**: The step is very good. The step is also my best friend.  
**Pixel**: That’s one. I gave it a week before he met the step. I was being optimistic.  

#### `s21-tour`

**Clank**: Announcement: this is a POND! Announcement: this is a GATE! It sticks! Best friend!  
**Clank**: Announcement: I am announcing!  
_You go round roots and kerbs, not over them. On the flat path his one wheel whizzes. At the smallest bump, he wobbles._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what wheels are good at, and what they can’t do  
> _A wheel rolls instead of dragging, so on smooth, flat ground it needs only a small push._  
> _But a wheel can’t roll up something that sticks straight up, like a step. That’s why prams, wheelchairs and suitcases love a ramp._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wheels roll easily on smooth ground but struggle with steps and bumps._

_By the foot of the hill, every Nubbin in the Grove is following him in a line, like ducklings behind a teapot._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells you  
> _“Like ducklings behind a teapot.” What does that simile help you picture?_  
> - ✅ The Nubbins follow him in a neat little line, and he’s round and warm like a teapot. → Yes! Two pictures in one: a wobbly line of followers, and a round, warm, whistling leader.
> - The Nubbins are actually ducks. → Ha! They’re still Nubbins. The simile says they follow him LIKE ducklings: in a neat little line behind a round, warm teapot.
> - Clank is making tea. → Not today. The simile compares him to a teapot because he’s round and warm, with a line of little followers behind.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile helps the reader picture._

_One climbs onto his hood. Then three. He turns his chimney-light down low for them, and they purr._  
**Clank**: They like me. Announcement: they LIKE me.  
**Clank**: I didn’t know that was available.  

#### `s21-help`

_You are woken at dawn by a whistle going up and up, and an announcement right outside your bedroom window._  
**Clank**: GOOD MORNING, BEST FRIEND! I have done SO MUCH HELPING!  
_Fern is in her garden in her dressing gown, holding her cat at arm’s length. Mustard is soaked, and furious about it._  
**Fern**: He watered Mustard. He watered my cat. In fairness, Mustard was in the beans. And he is a bit bean-coloured.  
**Clank**: Cats are plants that run! I looked it up! In my head!  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, ask): how plants and animals get food  
> _Clank says cats are plants that run. Is he right?_  
> - ✅ No. A cat is an animal. It eats its food and moves about. → Right. Plants make their own food, using sunlight, air and water. Cats have to eat theirs. Both need water, which is the one thing Clank got right. Just not poured on the outside.
> - Yes. Cats are plants. → Mustard would like a word. Plants make their own food from sunlight, air and water. Cats eat theirs. So a cat is an animal.
> - A cat is a kind of bean. → He is bean-coloured. I’ll give you that. But beans are plants that make their own food from sunlight. Cats eat theirs. Mustard is an animal.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a difference between plants (make their own food) and animals (eat food), while noting both need water._

_Behind her, Fern’s one good apple tree has been pruned. Carefully. Thoroughly. Into the shape of a duck._  
**Fern**: That’s the wrong tree. The ones I’m keeping alive, badly, have never looked better. That one was my good one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): helping by asking first  
> _Clank really wanted to help. But helping works best when you ask first: “Would you like me to…?”_  
> _Then you help with what the person actually needs. Fern needed the beans watered. Not the cat._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real helping starts with asking what someone needs._

_Then you notice the western hill. The small old shape that is always on top of it isn’t there._  
**Clank**: Also! I rescued a little old one! He was stranded up the hill! For HOURS! He wasn’t even MOVING!  
_Speeding round the pond at what can only be called full kettle is Clank._  
_He is holding the little grey watcher from the hill out in front of him, like a pie._  

#### `s21-moss`

_You catch up with Clank at the cottage. So does the step._  
_Clank goes over the edge. The little grey one leaves his hands, turns once in the air, and lands on his feet, as if he’d planned the morning._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): balanced and unbalanced forces: why things fall off edges  
> **Pixel**: On flat ground, gravity pulls him down and the ground pushes back up. The pushes balance, so he stays put.  
> **Pixel**: Off the edge, nothing pushes up. The forces are unbalanced. Gravity wins. Down he goes. Every time.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that balanced forces keep an object still, and unbalanced forces (like gravity with nothing pushing back) make it move._

**Clank**: Announcement… I have found the step again.  
_He looks at you for a long time. It’s the look of something very old that has been carried round a pond like a pie._  
_Then he turns and walks back up the hill, very dignified. It takes him the rest of the morning. He doesn’t look back once._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading a silent character’s body language  
> _The little grey one doesn’t say a word. What do his long look and his slow walk away tell you?_  
> - ✅ He wasn’t pleased, but he’s far too dignified to make a fuss. → Good reading. A long look and a walk with no looking back can say more than shouting. He has been carried like a pie, and he has feelings about it.
> - He loved the ride and wants another go. → If he loved it, he might stay! He walks all the way back without looking round. That says: not pleased, but too dignified to fuss.
> - He’s lost. → He knows exactly where he’s going: back to the top of his hill. The slow, proud walk says he wasn’t pleased.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a silent character’s feelings from his actions and body language._

**Pixel**: That’s two.  

#### `s21-log`

_That afternoon Byte is at the gate with a clipboard, a pencil behind each ear, and the face of someone who has made a table._  
**Byte**: Incident log. Since breakfast: one wet cat. One duck-shaped tree. One old Nubbin, moved at about eleven miles an hour.  
**Byte**: Two falls down the step. Fourteen announcements of best friendship. One of them to a bucket.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.D.10, do): making and reading a tally chart  
> **Byte**: Help me turn my log into a tally chart. One row each: wet cats, duck trees, carried Nubbins, falls, best friends.  
> **Byte**: Tally marks go in fives: four lines, then one across. Which row is longest?  
> Check: `edu:make:tally-chart:incident-log`
> _For grown-ups: Made a tally chart from a list of events (1, 1, 1, 2, 14) and found the largest category._

**Byte**: He’s a kettle on a wheel who wants to help. That is exactly how accidents introduce themselves.  
**Byte**: Next time it’s a Nubbin he waters. Or drops. Pixel should switch Clank off. Tonight. Before he hurts someone.  
_Behind you, a small whistle starts to rise, and stops halfway._  
_Clank is at the top of the cottage step. He has heard all of it. His chimney-light has gone very dim._  
_He reverses. He goes off the step backwards, lands in the thyme, and doesn’t announce anything at all._  
**Pixel**: …That’s three.  
_By the time you reach the step he’s gone. There’s just a wheel-track through the herbs, heading for the lantern shed._  
**Byte**: I didn’t know he could hear. I didn’t know he could… mind.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): what makes something alive; can a robot be a friend (think question)  
> _Byte didn’t know Clank could mind. What do you think? Is Clank alive? Can a robot be a real friend?_  
> - He’s a machine, so he isn’t alive. But he can still be a friend. → That’s a fair answer. Scientists say living things grow, need food and water, and make young. Clank does none of those. But being a friend is about how you treat each other. He’s very good at that part.
> - He might be alive. He has feelings. → That’s a fair answer. Clank seems to mind things, and that matters. A scientist would say he doesn’t grow, eat or make young. Nobody is quite sure what his feelings are made of. Not even Pixel.
> - He’s a tool, like a watering can. → That’s a fair answer. He was built to do jobs. But a watering can doesn’t hide when its feelings are hurt. Maybe Clank is something new: a tool who wants to be a friend.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes something alive (growing, needing food and water, making young) and whether a robot can be a friend._


**Choices**

- **Tell Byte he had a point. Clank does need to learn.**
    - **Byte**: I did have a point. I hate that I had a point. It’s much worse having one when it hurts.
    - **Pixel**: Something between “on” and “kettle”. That’s all he needs. I can build that.
- **Tell Byte that wasn’t fair. He’s only days old.**
    - **Byte**: Days old. I didn’t count that in.
    - **Byte**: I was days old once. I’m told I bit a vicar.

#### `s21-shed`

_The lantern shed smells of paraffin and old string. Clank is on the back shelf among the spare chimneys, pretending to be a lantern._  
_He is very bad at it. Lanterns don’t shake._  
**Clank**: Announcement. I’m a lantern now. Lanterns are useful. Nobody switches off a lantern.  
**Clank**: Except in the morning. They do switch them off in the morning.  
**Clank**: Byte’s right. I watered a cat. I made a tree into a duck. I carried the old one too fast and he didn’t say one single thing.  
**Clank**: Am I a friend? Or am I a thing that does jobs?  
**Clank**: Because if it’s jobs, I can do jobs better. I can learn. But if I stop being useful…  
**Clank**: If I stop being useful, will you still…  
_He stops. Something inside him clicks, and clicks again, looking for a word it hasn’t got._  
**Clank**: I don’t have the word. Pixel didn’t put it in.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): putting a word to a worry  
> _“If I stop being useful, will you still…” Which word do you think Clank is looking for?_  
> - …like me? → That could be it. Clank is worried: scared about something that might happen. Finding the word for a worry makes it easier to share.
> - …want me? → That could be it. Clank is worried he only matters when he’s doing jobs. Saying a worry out loud is the first step to someone helping.
> - …love me? → That could be it. It’s a big word for a small kettle. Clank is worried. Naming a worry is brave, even if you need help finding the word.
> _For grown-ups: Helped a character find words for a worry, and learned that naming a worry makes it easier to share._


**Choices**

- **Sit down below the shelf, and wait.**
    - You sit on the shed floor under the shelf. It isn’t comfortable. You stay.
    - **Clank**: What are you doing? Is it a job?
    - **You**: No. I’m just here.
    - **Clank**: Just here for what?
    - **You**: Nothing. That’s the whole thing.
    - After a long time Clank comes down off the shelf, very carefully, and parks beside you. He doesn’t announce it.
- **Teach him the step: it’s all right to ask for help.**
    - **You**: Do you know why you keep falling down the step?
    - **Clank**: Because I am brave?
    - **You**: Because you never ask anyone to help you down it.
    - **Clank**: But then I’d be needing. Helpers don’t need. Needing is the opposite of a job.
    - **You**: Everybody needs a hand with a step sometimes. Fern does. Hazel did. I do, on bad days.
    - Clank thinks about this for so long that his whistle goes off by itself, very softly.

#### `s21-ramp`

_Next afternoon Byte comes up the lane with a plank, a saw, and the face of a sum that won’t come out._  
**Byte**: I measured the step. Nineteen centimetres. The safe height for one wheel is, as far as I can find, zero.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): choosing a sensible unit of length  
> _Byte says the step is nineteen… what? Which unit makes sense for a step?_  
> - ✅ Centimetres → Yes. 19 cm is about the length of a pencil. A good size for a step, and a bad size for one wheel.
> - Metres → 19 metres is taller than a house! That would be quite a step. For a step, centimetres make sense: 19 cm.
> - Kilometres → 19 kilometres would take about four hours to walk! For a step, centimetres make sense: 19 cm.
> _For grown-ups: Chose centimetres as the sensible unit for a step’s height, comparing it with metres and kilometres._

**Byte**: So it isn’t him. Statistically, it’s the step.  
**Byte**: I said he should be switched off. That was a conclusion. I hadn’t finished collecting the data.  
**Byte**: The data now includes eleven Nubbins who follow him everywhere. That is a significant result.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-2-ETS1-1, notice): defining the real problem before fixing it  
> _Byte has changed the problem. Not “Clank keeps falling”, but “the step is too high for a wheel”._  
> _Engineers and scientists work like this. Say exactly what the problem is, look at all the data, and change your mind when the data changes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that solving a problem starts with defining it clearly, and that good thinkers change their minds when new evidence arrives._

**Clank**: Byte! Byte! Does that mean you’re my best—  
**Byte**: Provisionally.  

#### `s21-down`

_The ramp is finished: small, sanded, very well made. Byte calls it an inclined plane. Everyone else calls it a ramp._  
**Clank**: Announcement. I am going down the step.  
**Clank**: Announcement. Would somebody… come with me? The first time?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for help is brave  
> _That might be the bravest thing Clank has done. He asked for help._  
> _Asking isn’t the opposite of being helpful. It’s how everybody gets down hard steps. Robots included._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that asking for help is a brave and normal thing to do._

_Byte puts one hand on his hood. You put one on the other side. Pixel holds the wheelbarrow, for reasons._  
_He goes down the ramp at the speed of a snail with doubts. He reaches the bottom. Nothing falls._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): why a ramp (inclined plane) is gentler than a step  
> _Why can Clank go down the ramp safely, when the step always tipped him over?_  
> - ✅ The ramp spreads the drop over a long, gentle slope, so he goes down a little at a time. → Yes. Gravity still pulls, but the slope means it pulls him gently along instead of straight down all at once. A steeper ramp would make him go faster. Byte checked. Eleven times.
> - Ramps switch gravity off. → Gravity never switches off! The ramp spreads the drop out over a long slope, so gravity pulls him down gently, a little at a time.
> - It’s magic. → It feels like magic! But it’s a simple machine: a slope spreads the drop out, so gravity takes him down gently, a bit at a time.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a ramp (inclined plane) spreads a drop over a longer distance, so gravity moves an object down more gently._

**Clank**: I DID THE STEP! I did the step and I didn’t find it!  
_He does a little dance: forward, back, a spin on his one wheel. You copy it. Byte copies it, and later denies it._  
**Pixel**: That’s… none. I’ll take none.  

#### `s21-evening`

_The afternoon goes gold. Clank parks at the bottom of the new ramp and doesn’t water anything, which costs him a great deal._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why evening sunlight looks golden  
> _Why does the afternoon go gold? When the Sun is low, its light travels through much more air to reach you._  
> _The air scatters away lots of the blue light on the way. What gets through looks warm and golden._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that low evening sunlight passes through more air, which scatters blue light, so it looks golden._

**Clank**: Announcement: I am not helping. I am just… here.  
**Clank**: Is that allowed? Is just here allowed?  
**You**: Just here is allowed.  
**Clank**: Announcement: just here is allowed.  
_He twitches towards a dandelion. He stops himself. It is the hardest thing he has done all week._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, do): being still and noticing  
> _Be “just here” with Clank. Sit still and listen._  
> _Can you hear three different sounds? Maybe a bird, the pond, and a very small kettle-whistle trying not to happen._  
> Check: `edu:listen:sounds:3`
> _For grown-ups: Practised sitting still and noticing three sounds, a simple calming exercise._


#### `s21-complete`

_At dusk the Nubbins come in from the long grass one by one, and climb onto Clank, because he’s warm, like a kettle that’s just been on._  
_Seven of them. Eight. One on his wheel. One perched on his lantern hood, like a hat._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from warmer things to cooler things  
> _Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things. As dusk cools the air, Clank’s warmth flows into the Nubbins snuggled on him._  
> _That’s why they choose him. He’s the warmest seat in the Grove._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from warmer objects to cooler ones._

**Clank**: Announcement.  
**Clank**: I am being very still.  
_He is. For an hour, the chattiest thing in the valley doesn’t move a bolt. Not even to announce that he isn’t moving._  
_You sit beside him. That’s all. It turns out that’s plenty._  
**Pixel**: Keep him. He’s yours now. He’ll water things, slowly. Mostly plants.  
_Pixel drops a spare lantern hood on your head. It fits, as if it was waiting to._  
_Next morning he is out among the beans with a watering can, one bean a minute. Mustard watches from Fern’s wall, from very far away._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): a time interval: one bean a minute  
> _Clank waters one bean a minute. There are 30 beans in the row. How long will the whole row take?_  
> - ✅ 30 minutes → Yes! One a minute, 30 beans: 30 minutes. That’s half an hour of very loud watering.
> - 3 minutes → That would be ten beans a minute, and Clank is a one-bean-a-minute robot. 30 beans takes 30 minutes: half an hour.
> - 30 hours → He’s slow, but not that slow! One bean a minute means 30 beans take 30 minutes: half an hour.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval (30 beans at one a minute takes 30 minutes, half an hour)._

_Clank is still a machine. He is also, it turns out, somebody’s friend. Both things can be true at once._  

### Glossary

- **optimistic**: Hoping and expecting that things will turn out well.
- **announcement**: Something said out loud so that everyone knows it.
- **pruned**: Cut back, to trim a plant or tree into shape.
- **stranded**: Stuck somewhere with no way to get back.
- **dignified**: Calm and proud, even when something silly happens.
- **incident**: Something that happens, often something that goes wrong.
- **paraffin**: A kind of oil that is burned in lamps and lanterns.
- **data**: Facts and measurements collected so you can find something out.
- **provisionally**: For now, until it is checked or decided for sure.
- **inclined plane**: A flat surface set at a slope: a ramp. It is one of the simple machines.

## Q1. Two Shrubberies

- `q01-s1`: Make a shrubbery at the Workshop and give it to the hooded three. · _The Workshop makes a shrubbery from reeds and wood. Carry it to the falls and use Give._
- `q01-s2`: Make a second shrubbery, a little higher, with a beetle-sized path, and place it by the first. · _Craft another shrubbery and a path tile, then place both beside the first with the Decorate tool._

#### `q01-intro`

_The waterfall path is blocked. Three Nubbins in long brown hoods stand shoulder to shoulder, which for Nubbins means elbow to elbow._  
_The middle one is taller than the others. Look closer: it is standing on a log._  
**The Hooded Three**: GRONK!  
_Your Nubbin flinches. A small bird leaves a nearby tree and does not come back._  
**You**: Could we just get past, please?  
**The Tall Hood**: You may not. Not until you bring us the one thing our hearts are set on.  
_There is a long pause, full of suspense. Everyone waits to hear what comes next. The hoods sway._  
**The Tall Hood**: It is green. It is leafy. It is… a bush. A tidy little bush. A shrubbery.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): how writers build suspense  
> _Look at the Tall Hood’s words: “It is… a bush.”_  
> _Why do you think the writer put “…” before the big reveal?_  
> - ✅ To make us wait and wonder: suspense. → Yes. The dots are a pause. A pause makes the reader lean in and wonder what is coming. Then the answer lands: a bush. The bigger the pause, the sillier the answer feels.
> - Because the Tall Hood forgot the word. → Ha! It might have. But here the dots are on purpose. They make a pause, so we wait and wonder. That waiting feeling is called suspense. Writers use it right before a surprise.
> - It doesn’t mean anything. → Read it aloud and stop at the dots. Hear the wait? That pause builds suspense. Writers use “…” to make us lean in before a surprise. Here, the surprise is a bush.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a pause (written “…”) builds suspense before a big reveal._

_The other two nod gravely. One of them was not expecting it and nods a moment late._  

**Choices**

- **What sort of shrubbery?**
    - **The Tall Hood**: A tidy one. About knee-high, on a Nubbin. With leaves. Leaves are important.
    - The hood on the left whispers something. The Tall Hood adds, firmly: “Green.”
- **Chant back at them.**
    - You make the loudest, strangest noise you can manage.
    - The hooded three look at one another. The one on the right writes something down.
- **One shrubbery. Coming up.**
    - **The Tall Hood**: Good. We shall wait here. Swaying.

#### `q01-first`

_You set the shrubbery down by the falls. It is a neat little bush of reeds and twigs, with fresh leaves._  
_The hooded three lean over it and inspect it from every side, including underneath._  
_To inspect something is to look at it very carefully. They take this seriously. One uses a magnifying leaf._  
**The Tall Hood**: This shrubbery pleases us. It has leaves. We approve of the leaves.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): what a shrub is, and what leaves do  
> **The Tall Hood**: Do you know what makes a shrub a shrub? Woody stems. Lots of them, all from near the ground.  
> **The Tall Hood**: A tree usually has one big trunk and grows much taller. A shrub stays low and bushy.  
> **The Tall Hood**: And the leaves are the kitchen. They use sunlight, air and water to make the plant’s food.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a shrub is a woody plant with many stems, and that leaves use sunlight to make a plant’s food._

**The Tall Hood**: A shrubbery without leaves is just a pile of sticks with ideas.  
_They chant once more, softly, as a kind of thank-you. The bird does not come back for that either._  

#### `q01-second`

_You step towards the path. The Tall Hood raises one paw._  
**The Tall Hood**: Wait. There is a second thing.  
**You**: You said one shrubbery.  
**The Tall Hood**: We did. We have grown since then. As people.  
**The Tall Hood**: Bring us another. It goes next to this one, but up a step, so the two look terraced, like stairs up a hill.  
**The Tall Hood**: And a small path between them. Not a big path. The sort of path a beetle would enjoy.  
_The other two hoods nod. One holds its paws a beetle-width apart, to help._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.A.1, do): measure length in centimetres  
> **The Tall Hood**: Measure the gap between my colleague’s paws. Use the ruler from your bag. Line up the zero.  
> _The gap is 2 centimetres: about as wide as a beetle walking along with its legs out._  
> **The Tall Hood**: Excellent. A metre is 100 of those. That would be a path for a horse. We are not catering for horses.  
> Check: `edu:measure:beetle-path:2cm`
> _For grown-ups: Measured a beetle-sized path with a ruler (2 cm) and compared centimetres with metres._

**You**: And then we can pass?  
**The Tall Hood**: Then we shall discuss it.  
**The Tall Hood**: Also, we are no longer the Hooded Three. We have a new name. It goes like this.  
_It makes a noise like a tea tray falling down a staircase full of spoons. The other two join in, slightly behind._  
**You**: I can’t say that.  
**The Tall Hood**: Nobody can. That is what makes it so frightening.  

**Choices**

- **Fine. A little higher, with a path.**
    - **The Tall Hood**: Good. Use gravel. We have strong feelings about gravel.
- **Can the path be imaginary?**
    - **The Tall Hood**: No. We tried that once. Somebody fell off it.

#### `q01-terraced`

_Two shrubberies, one a little higher than the other, with a tiny gravel path wandering between them._  
_It is, you have to admit, rather lovely._  
**The Tall Hood**: Oh. Oh, that is nice.  
_Just then a rain cloud drifts over the falls and lets go. Everyone huddles under the hoods’ hoods._  
_The rain runs down the hill. On the terrace it slows, soaks in, and stays where the roots are._  
**The Tall Hood**: Look at that. The water is staying put. Our steps are doing a job.  
_Below the path, on the bare slope, a little stream of muddy water carries soil away._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): how terraces and roots slow erosion  
> _When rain rushes down a bare slope, it carries soil with it. That slow wearing away of land is called erosion._  
> _Flat steps called terraces slow the water down, and plant roots hold the soil together._  
> _Farmers in hilly places have built terraces for thousands of years, for exactly this reason._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that terraces and plant roots slow rainwater so it does not wash soil away (erosion)._


#### `q01-complete`

_The hooded three step aside. Then they step back again, because they want to keep looking at the shrubbery._  
**The Tall Hood**: You may pass. You may pass every day, in fact. We shall be here.  
**You**: Here? For good?  
**The Tall Hood**: There is a terrace, and a path. Where else would we go?  
**The Tall Hood**: We guarded this path for years, you know. We never once asked what was at the other end of it.  
**The Tall Hood**: A shrubbery is a much better reason to stand somewhere.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think question: doing things just because we always have  
> **The Tall Hood**: We stood here for years, guarding a path, and never asked why.  
> **The Tall Hood**: Why do you think someone keeps doing a thing for years without asking what it is for?  
> - Because it’s a habit, and habits are comfy. → Yes. A habit is like a well-worn path. Your feet follow it without asking your head. That is a fair answer. We were very comfy. We just weren’t happy.
> - Because nobody told them to stop. → That is a fair answer. Nobody did tell us. And we never told ourselves. Sometimes you have to be your own somebody.
> - Maybe they were scared of what was at the other end. → Oh. That is a thoughtful answer. Perhaps we were. Guarding a path is easier than walking it. A shrubbery gave us a braver reason to stay.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people keep doing something out of habit, and what it means to find a better reason._

_They settle on a flat rock by the falls. One produces a tiny rake and starts tidying the gravel._  
_The terraced shrubbery is yours to move anywhere you like. They hope you won’t. They will forgive you if you do._  
_At dusk you can hear them practising their new name. They have still not got all the way through it._  

### Glossary

- **suspense**: The excited, waiting feeling when you want to know what happens next.
- **inspect**: To look at something very carefully, checking every part.
- **terraced**: Built in flat steps, one a little higher than the next, like stairs up a hill.
- **erosion**: The slow wearing away of land by water, wind or ice.

## Q2. The Plank Knight

- `q02-s1`: Beat Sir Dentwhistle at karate on the plank bridge. · _Choose Karate on the bridge to start a bout. Any of your Nubbins can take part._
- `q02-s2`: Win a second bout against Sir Dentwhistle. · _Same bridge. Swap in a fresher Nubbin if yours is tired; Sir Dentwhistle does not mind._
- `q02-s3`: Win the third and final bout. · _If you keep losing, rest your Nubbin first. Tired Nubbins move slowly._

#### `q02-intro`

_A plank bridge crosses the stream. In the middle of it stands a Power Nubbin in a dented tin helmet, perfectly still._  
_It has stood there so long that a snail has started up its leg. It has not noticed, or will not admit it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how a snail moves  
> _How does a snail climb a knight? Slowly, and on one big foot._  
> _A snail’s body is mostly one long, muscly foot. Tiny waves ripple along it and push the snail forward._  
> _It also makes slime, which helps it grip and glide. Even up a leg that would rather it didn’t._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a snail glides on one muscly foot, over a layer of slime it makes itself._

**You**: Excuse me. We’d like to cross.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Halt! This plank is closed to the public, and you are extremely public.  
_Its voice echoes inside the helmet. It sounds like someone talking into a bucket._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: I am Sir Dentwhistle. I have guarded this plank for three whole days.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Before that it was unguarded. Chaos. People simply walked across it.  
_It raises its little fists. If you want to cross, you will have to beat it at karate._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: I warn you, I am extremely courteous. I shall bow first, and then defeat you.  

**Choices**

- **Bow politely, then fight.**
    - **Sir Dentwhistle**: A bow! Now we are both courteous. This will be the politest defeat in history.
    - In real karate, people bow before and after a bout. It means: I respect you, and I will play fair.
- **Can’t we just go round?**
    - You look downstream. There is a perfectly good row of stepping stones about ten steps away.
    - **Sir Dentwhistle**: Nobody uses those. They are beneath us. Literally. They are lower.

#### `q02-round1`

_Your Nubbin’s best move sends the dented helmet spinning off into the grass. Bonk. Roll. Stop._  
_Underneath, Sir Dentwhistle has very flat hair._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Barely a bump! I hardly felt a thing!  
**You**: It was your hat.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: A hat is a sort of bump. A bump on the head. Again!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character traits from what a character says and does  
> _Sir Dentwhistle just lost its helmet. It says it was “barely a bump”._  
> _What trait does that show? What is it like?_  
> - ✅ It is proud, and hates admitting it lost. → Exactly. Its words say “fine”. Its pink ears say “embarrassed”. When words and actions don’t match, the actions often tell the truth.
> - It really didn’t feel anything. → Its head is fine, true. But look at its ears: pink. It feels something. Embarrassment. It is proud and won’t admit it lost. That’s a character trait: something it does again and again.
> - It is very brave. → It is brave, in a way! But calling it “barely a bump” shows something else too. It is proud and hates admitting a loss. Watch for it: it will do it again.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s trait (proud, won’t admit losing) from its words and its pink ears._

_Its ears have gone pink. The snail stops climbing, out of tact._  

#### `q02-scarf`

_Sir Dentwhistle wraps a long woollen scarf round its neck three times, for armour._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: The scarf is my second line of defence. Nobody has ever got past the scarf.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: My mother knitted it. She said nothing would ever get through it. She meant the cold, but the principle stands.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): insulation: wool traps warmth  
> **Sir Dentwhistle**: My mother called it insulation. Tell me, Keeper: where does a scarf’s warmth actually come from?  
> - ✅ From you. The wool keeps your own warmth in. → Correct! Wool is full of tiny pockets of trapped air. Heat struggles to get through them. So my warmth stays with me. That is called insulation. My mother was an expert.
> - The wool makes heat by itself. → A popular idea! But no. Put a scarf on a cold stone, and the stone stays cold. Wool traps air, and air keeps your own body’s warmth in. That is called insulation.
> - From the sun. → The sun warms many things. But a scarf works in the dark too. Its wool traps air, which keeps in the warmth my body makes. Insulation!
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a scarf doesn’t make heat; wool traps air and keeps in the body’s own warmth._

**You**: Has anybody tried?  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: That is not the point.  
_It takes up a fighting stance. The stance is mostly scarf._  
_The snail has reached its shoulder and is enjoying the view._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step length problem in centimetres  
> _Each wrap round Sir Dentwhistle’s small neck uses 20 centimetres of scarf. It wraps three times._  
> _Then 40 centimetres dangle down at the end. How long is the whole scarf?_  
> - ✅ 100 cm, which is 1 metre. → Yes. Three wraps of 20 is 60. Add the 40 hanging down: 100 centimetres. And 100 centimetres is exactly one metre. A metre of pure defence.
> - 60 cm → Good start: three wraps of 20 is 60. But don’t forget the bit dangling down. 60 add 40 is 100 centimetres. That’s one whole metre.
> - 63 cm → Careful: it’s three wraps of 20, so 20 + 20 + 20, which is 60. Then add the 40 that hangs down. 60 + 40 = 100 centimetres, or one metre.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: 3 wraps of 20 cm plus 40 cm left over makes 100 cm, or 1 metre._


#### `q02-round2`

_Your Nubbin grabs the end of the scarf and steps back. And back. And back._  
_The scarf unwinds in one long, satisfying pull and drifts off downstream like a woolly eel._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): similes  
> _“Like a woolly eel” is a simile: a comparison that uses “like” or “as”._  
> _An eel is a long, wriggly fish. Picture a wriggly fish made of wool. That’s the scarf._  
> _For grown-ups: Spotted a simile (“like a woolly eel”) and explained how comparing two things paints a picture._

**Sir Dentwhistle**: Barely bothered! I was getting warm anyway.  
_It puffs out three hot, cross breaths._  
_Its tiny round glasses fog up completely. It looks like a very small, very angry cloud._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, notice): condensation on cool glass  
> _Why did its glasses fog up? Breath is warm, and it carries water as an invisible gas: water vapour._  
> _When that warm, damp breath touches cooler glass, the vapour turns back into tiny drops of water._  
> _That change is called condensation. It’s the same thing that mists a bathroom mirror after a bath._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why glasses fog: water vapour in warm breath turns back into tiny drops on cooler glass._

**Sir Dentwhistle**: I can’t see a thing. This is not a disadvantage. It is a strategy.  

#### `q02-glasses`

_Sir Dentwhistle wipes its glasses on its own tummy and puts them back on, crooked._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Final round. I have one item left, and it is my best item.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Without these, I cannot see you. Which means you cannot see me either. Logically.  
**You**: That isn’t how seeing works.  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: It is how it works on my bridge.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see things when light from them reaches our eyes  
> **Sir Dentwhistle**: Prove it, then. If I take off my glasses, can you still see me?  
> - ✅ Yes. Light bounces off you into my eyes. → Exactly. Light hits Sir Dentwhistle, bounces off, and travels into your eyes. That’s how you see it. What it can see doesn’t change that at all. Its logic is wonky. Its plank is not exempt from science.
> - No, it’s right. → Try it! Close your own eyes. Can your Nubbin still see you? Of course it can. We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. What the other person sees doesn’t matter.
> - Only if it can see me first. → Seeing isn’t a swap. It only needs light: light bounces off Sir Dentwhistle and into your eyes. So you can see it whether its eyes are open, shut or fogged up.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that you see an object when light bounces off it into your eyes, whatever the object can see._

_Your Nubbin looks up at you. It would like to win quickly and then have a snack._  

**Choices**

- **Go easy on it.**
    - Your Nubbin nods and loosens its shoulders in a merciful way.
- **Give it everything.**
    - Your Nubbin cracks its knuckles. It has no knuckles. It cracks them anyway.

#### `q02-round3`

_The glasses fly off and land neatly in the snail’s path. The snail goes round them._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: I am completely fine. Never better. Which one of you said that? Both of you?  
_It is talking to a fence post._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Return at once! I have not finished being brave! I have barely started!  
_The fence post, to its credit, does not move an inch._  
_You pick up the glasses and gently put them back on Sir Dentwhistle’s nose. It blinks at you._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): glasses help eyes focus; eye tests  
> _Lots of people wear glasses, from small children to grandparents. They help eyes focus, so things look sharp._  
> _If words or faces look blurry to you, tell a grown-up. An eye test is quick, and it doesn’t hurt._  
> **Sir Dentwhistle**: Mine were prescribed by a professional. I simply prefer to fight without them. Occasionally. By accident.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that glasses help eyes focus, and that blurry seeing is something to tell a grown-up about._

**Sir Dentwhistle**: Ah. There you are. You have moved. Sneaky.  

#### `q02-complete`

_Sir Dentwhistle sits down on the plank, which is the closest it will ever come to stepping aside._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Very well. You may cross. Not because you won. Because I am gracious, and I have decided to have a sit.  
_You pick the dented helmet out of the grass and offer it back. It pushes it towards you._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: Keep it. I have several others. At home. In a box.  
_It does not have several others. You can tell from the way it watches the helmet._  
**Sir Dentwhistle**: And tell your Nubbins this: losing is only losing if you mind. I never mind. I am famous for not minding.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): think question: plain truth or saving face  
> _Sir Dentwhistle lost three times, but won’t quite say so._  
> _Is it kinder to tell someone the plain truth, or to let them keep their pride?_  
> - The plain truth. Pretending doesn’t help anyone. → That’s a fair answer. Honest words, said gently, can be a gift. People often trust you more for them.
> - Let them keep their pride. Everyone needs that sometimes. → That’s a kind answer. Sometimes people need a soft landing first, and the truth later.
> - It depends on the person, and how you say it. → That’s a wise answer. A truth said kindly is very different from a truth said to win.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when it is kinder to tell someone a hard truth and when to let them keep their pride._

_You cross the plank in two steps. Downstream, the stepping stones look on, unused and faintly hurt._  
_From now on your Nubbins take karate losses the way Sir Dentwhistle does: cheerfully, and slightly wrongly._  

**Choices**

- **Shall we call it honours even?**
    - **Sir Dentwhistle**: Honours even. Yes. I was about to suggest it myself. I was being gracious.
    - It shakes your hand, and then the fence post’s, to be thorough.
- **You lost, you know. Three times.**
    - Sir Dentwhistle is quiet for a long moment. The snail, now on top of its head, is quiet too.
    - **Sir Dentwhistle**: …I know. I was there.
    - **Sir Dentwhistle**: Thank you for saying it plainly. Nobody ever does. It is oddly restful.

### Glossary

- **courteous**: Polite and respectful, even to someone you are competing against.
- **trait**: A quality that is part of someone’s character, like being proud, kind or stubborn.
- **insulation**: Material that stops heat getting in or out, like wool in a scarf.
- **simile**: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”, such as “drifts off like a woolly eel”.
- **condensation**: When water vapour (water as a gas) cools and turns back into drops of liquid water.
- **logically**: Following sensible steps of reasoning. Sir Dentwhistle uses the word without doing it.
- **gracious**: Kind and polite, especially when things haven’t gone your way.

## Q3. The Bridge of Three Questions

- `q03-s1`: Count every Nubbin in your Grove, then go back to the gorge. · _Open the counter and tap each Nubbin once. Use tally marks in fives. Don’t forget the ones in the pond._
- `q03-s2`: Find out how fast a Fly Nubbin can carry a coconut. · _Take a coconut from the palm on the coast, hand it to a Fly Nubbin and time its flight across the pond._

#### `q03-intro`

_At the edge of the gorge, beside a rope bridge nobody has ever been allowed on, sits a very old Keeper in a very old hood._  
_The hood has a fringe of moss. So, possibly, does the Keeper._  
**Old Gorrel**: Halt. Nobody sets foot on my bridge without answering three questions first.  
**Old Gorrel**: Answer rightly, and the bridge is yours. Answer wrongly, and… well. It is a long way down. To the stream.  
_You look down. The stream is knee-deep and full of contented ducks._  
**Old Gorrel**: First question. How many Nubbins live in your Grove? Exactly. Not roughly. I will know.  
**You**: I… think I know? Let me check.  
**Old Gorrel**: Go and count them. I shall wait. I am extremely good at waiting.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, do): tally marks in groups of five  
> **Old Gorrel**: A tip from an old counter. Use a tally. One line for each Nubbin.  
> **Old Gorrel**: Four lines standing up, then the fifth goes across them, like a little gate. That makes a group of five.  
> **Old Gorrel**: At the end, count the gates in fives, five, ten, fifteen, then add the loose lines. Much harder to lose your place.  
> Check: `edu:tally:nubbins:fives`
> _For grown-ups: Counted with tally marks in fives, then counted the groups (5, 10, 15…) to find the total quickly._


**Choices**

- **Make a confident guess.**
    - **Old Gorrel**: Wrong. Probably. A guess is not an answer. Go and count.
- **Go and count properly.**
    - **Old Gorrel**: Wise. The last one who guessed is still in the stream. He likes it there now.

#### `q03-count`

_You come back with the number, tally and all. Old Gorrel checks it against something written on his sleeve._  
**Old Gorrel**: Correct. Annoyingly.  
**Old Gorrel**: Second question. What did your newest Nubbin eat for breakfast?  
**You**: A run fruit. Half of one. It dropped the other half in the pond.  
**Old Gorrel**: Correct, and also tragic.  
_Down in the stream, a duck finds the floating half, eats it, and then spends a long time tidying its feathers._  
**Old Gorrel**: Ducks. Always preening. Vain creatures. Dry, though. Always dry.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how ducks keep their feathers waterproof  
> **Old Gorrel**: It isn’t vanity, really. Near its tail a duck has a small gland that makes oil.  
> **Old Gorrel**: When it preens, it rubs that oil all over its feathers with its beak. Water rolls straight off.  
> **Old Gorrel**: That is why a duck can sit in a stream all day and still be dry underneath. I envy it.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that ducks spread oil from a gland near the tail over their feathers to keep them waterproof._


#### `q03-third`

**Old Gorrel**: Third question.  
_He leans forward. The hood leans further. The ducks below go quiet, sensing an occasion._  
**Old Gorrel**: Read this card. Out loud. It is very old.  
_The card says: “How quickly can a small bird fly, with nothing at all in its claws?”_  
**You**: Birds aren’t really my area.  
**Old Gorrel**: Nor mine. I have never actually seen the bird on the card.  
**Old Gorrel**: Then a Fly Nubbin. Carrying a coconut. How fast? Go and find out.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): speed needs distance and time  
> **Old Gorrel**: Before you go, Keeper. To find the speed of something, how fast it goes, what must you measure?  
> - ✅ How far it goes, and how long it takes. → Yes. Distance and time. Say the pond is 20 metres across and it takes 10 seconds. Then it flies 2 metres every second. That’s its speed. Off you go.
> - How heavy the coconut is. → The coconut might slow it down, true. But you can’t get speed from weight alone. Speed needs distance and time: how far, and how long. Measure the pond, then time the flight.
> - Just how long it takes. → Half right! But 10 seconds to cross a puddle is slow, and 10 seconds to cross a lake is fast. You need both: how far it goes, and how long it takes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that to measure speed you need two measurements: how far something goes, and how long it takes._

_He sits back, smug as a cushion. Nobody has ever answered the third question._  

#### `q03-timed`

_You pace out the pond: 20 metres. Then you time two Fly Nubbins, one at a time, with the same coconut._  
_The first carries the coconut briskly across the pond. Ten seconds._  
_The second carries it halfway, sits on it, and has a think. Then it finishes. Forty seconds._  
_You try each of them again, just to be sure. The first: eleven seconds. The second: it sits again. Same spot._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): fair tests and repeating trials  
> _You used the same pond and the same coconut for both Nubbins. Then you did it all twice._  
> _Why was that a good idea?_  
> - ✅ So the only difference was the Nubbin, and so one odd result can’t fool me. → Exactly. Keeping everything else the same makes it a fair test: only one thing changes. And repeating it shows whether a result was a fluke. Real scientists do both.
> - It wasn’t needed. Once is enough. → Once can fool you! The second Nubbin might have sat down just once, by chance. Doing it twice showed it sits every time. And using the same pond and coconut kept the test fair.
> - So the Nubbins got more exercise. → They did! But there’s a science reason too. Same pond, same coconut: only the Nubbin changes, so it’s a fair test. Repeating shows if a result was luck.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what makes a test fair (change only one thing) and why scientists repeat a test._

_So the honest answer is: it depends on the Fly Nubbin._  
_You write both answers down, like a proper fair test. You have a feeling that is the whole point._  

#### `q03-complete`

**Old Gorrel**: Well? How fast?  
**You**: That depends. Do you mean the Fly Nubbin that zooms, or the one that stops for a sit halfway?  
_Old Gorrel opens his mouth. Then he closes it. Then he opens it again, to check it still works._  
**Old Gorrel**: I… don’t know that. Nobody has ever asked me one back.  
_He takes a thoughtful step backwards, onto nothing in particular, and drops neatly into the stream._  
_There is a splash, and then a great deal of indignant quacking. The ducks are cross, but nobody is hurt._  
**Old Gorrel**: I’m all right! It’s rather pleasant, actually! The bridge is yours!  
**Old Gorrel**: Forty years of asking people questions. Do you know, it’s rather lovely to be asked one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think question: is it good to be asked a question you can’t answer?  
> **Old Gorrel**: I didn’t know the answer, and I fell in a stream. And yet I feel wonderful. What do you make of that?  
> - Not knowing is exciting. Now there’s something new to find out. → That is a fair answer. Forty years of knowing all the answers was rather dull, now you mention it.
> - Maybe he was lonely, and a question back felt like a real conversation. → Oh. That’s a thoughtful answer. A question back means someone is really listening.
> - I’d feel embarrassed if I didn’t know. → That’s honest, and lots of people feel that way. I did, for about one second. Then the water was nice. Not knowing is where all the learning starts.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how it feels not to know an answer, and why asking questions back can be a good thing._

_He floats away on his back, waving. Halfway, he flings his hood up onto the rope post. It lands perfectly. He has practised._  

### Glossary

- **tally**: A way of counting with lines, crossing every fifth one to make groups of five.
- **preening**: When a bird cleans and tidies its feathers with its beak.
- **speed**: How far something travels in a certain amount of time, such as 2 metres every second.
- **fair test**: A test where you change only one thing, so you know that thing made the difference.
- **indignant**: Cross because you feel something unfair or rude has happened.

## Q4. Clip-Clop

- `q04-s1`: Find out where the coconut shells came from. · _Follow the coast path to the one palm tree and look for whoever has been carrying fruit away from it._
- `q04-s2`: Decide what happens to the coconut shells. · _Go back to the lookout wall. The Run Nubbin will follow; talk to it there._

#### `q04-intro`

_Clop. Clop-clop. Clop._  
_Behind you, a Run Nubbin is trotting in step with you, banging two coconut half-shells together._  
_When you stop, it stops. When you walk, it clops. It looks extremely pleased with the arrangement._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): sounds are made by vibrations  
> _Clop! When the shells hit, they vibrate. How does that make a sound you can hear from up on the wall?_  
> - ✅ The shaking passes through the air to our ears. → Yes. When the shells knock together they vibrate: they shake very fast, back and forth. That shaking passes through the air to your ears. Hollow shells make a big, round clop.
> - The sound is stored inside the coconut. → A lovely idea! But an empty shell has no sound stored inside. The sound happens when the shells hit and vibrate: shake very fast. The air carries that shaking to your ears.
> - The Run Nubbin is just saying “clop”. → Ha! It does look the type. But the clop comes from the shells. When they knock together, they vibrate. The vibration travels through the air to your ears.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the shells make a sound because they vibrate when they hit, shaking the air all the way to our ears._

_Up on the lookout wall, Warden Ollery leans over with a telescope, which at this distance is no help at all._  
**Warden Ollery**: Those shells. Wherever did they come from?  
**You**: They aren’t mine. They’re… its.  
**Warden Ollery**: Coconuts don’t grow round here. One palm in the whole valley, and that’s on the coast.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): coconuts float, which helps palms spread  
> **Warden Ollery**: Funny things, coconuts. A coconut is a seed in a big, hard, hairy case. And it floats.  
> **Warden Ollery**: The sea can carry one for weeks. If it washes up on a warm beach, it can sprout into a new palm.  
> **Warden Ollery**: That’s probably how our one lonely palm got here. It sailed.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that coconuts float, so the sea can carry them to new beaches where they grow into palms._

**Warden Ollery**: So how did they get all the way up here? I’ve been wondering since breakfast.  
**Warden Ollery**: Unless two Fly Nubbins carried it between them. On a bit of string. Holding one end each.  
_He thinks about this for slightly longer than is healthy, then draws a diagram on the wall in chalk._  
_The Run Nubbin clops twice, which might mean anything._  

**Choices**

- **Ask the Run Nubbin.**
    - It clops, then points its whole body towards the sea.
- **Does it matter?**
    - **Warden Ollery**: Everything matters, from up here. There’s not much else to look at.

#### `q04-gullwick`

_Under the palm sits a Fly Nubbin with enormous, exhausted wings. Its name tag says Gullwick._  
**Gullwick**: Carried it. All the way. Uphill. Into a headwind.  
_A headwind is wind that blows straight into your face, the opposite way to where you’re going._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): forces: pushing against the wind  
> _Why does flying into a headwind make Gullwick so tired?_  
> - ✅ The wind pushes back, so it has to push harder. → Exactly. Gullwick’s wings push forward, and the wind pushes backward. Two forces, fighting. To move at all, Gullwick has to push harder than the wind. That takes a lot of energy.
> - Wind makes the coconut heavier. → The coconut weighs the same in any wind. But the wind does push against Gullwick. Wings push forward, wind pushes back. Gullwick must push harder than the wind to get anywhere.
> - It isn’t harder. Wind helps you fly. → A wind behind you helps: that’s a tailwind. A headwind blows the other way, into your face. It pushes back against the wings, so Gullwick has to work much harder.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a headwind makes travel harder: the wind pushes the opposite way, so you must push harder._

**Gullwick**: Dropped it on a rock at the top. Went in two. Run Nubbin found the halves. Very happy. I am very tired.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: halves and quarters  
> _The coconut split into two equal halves. Each half is 1/2._  
> _If it had smashed into four equal pieces instead, what fraction would each piece be?_  
> - ✅ 1/4, a quarter → Yes. Four equal pieces: each one is a quarter, 1/4. A quarter is smaller than a half. Trotwell would have had a much quieter clop.
> - 1/2 → 1/2 is one of two equal pieces. With four equal pieces, each is one of four: 1/4. More pieces means smaller pieces. A quarter is smaller than a half.
> - 4 → There would be 4 pieces, yes! But each piece is one out of four: 1/4, a quarter.
> _For grown-ups: Compared halves and quarters: the more equal pieces something is split into, the smaller each piece._

_Gullwick lies down flat in the sand to make the point._  
_Beside it lies another whole coconut, saved for later. Its wings twitch at the sight of it._  

**Choices**

- **Thank Gullwick properly.**
    - You thank Gullwick. It lifts one wing an inch off the sand, which is all the wing will do today.
    - **Gullwick**: Nobody said that before. Nice. Very tired. Still nice.
- **Why carry it all that way?**
    - **Gullwick**: Seemed like it wanted to go up.
    - It says this as though it explains everything. Possibly it does.

#### `q04-return`

_You walk back up to the lookout wall. Clop. Clop-clop. The Run Nubbin is right behind you, of course._  
**You**: A Fly Nubbin carried a whole coconut up from the coast. It broke on a rock.  
**Warden Ollery**: All that way? With those little wings?  
**Warden Ollery**: Well. Mystery solved. I suppose the shells ought to go back to the beach, really. Tidiness and so on.  
_The Run Nubbin hugs the shells to its chest and looks at you with its whole face._  
_It is the look of someone who has found the one sound they were born to make._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: when two people want different things  
> _Warden Ollery wants things tidy. The Run Nubbin loves its shells more than anything._  
> _Sometimes people find a compromise. Sometimes one gives way. How would you decide what’s fair?_  
> - Ask what matters most to each of them. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes one person cares a little and the other cares a lot. That helps you decide.
> - Find a way for both to get something. → That’s a thoughtful answer. People call that a compromise: nobody gets everything, but everybody gets something.
> - The shells were found, so finders keepers. → That’s an honest answer, and lots of people think that way. It’s worth asking, too: would anyone be hurt by it? Here, the beach probably won’t mind.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to decide fairly when two people want different things, and what each one cares about._


**Choices**

- **They’re yours. Keep them.**
    - The Run Nubbin does a small celebratory trot in a circle. Clop-clop-clop-clop.
- **Keep them, but let the others have a turn.**
    - The Run Nubbin considers this and agrees, provided its turn comes first. And last.

#### `q04-decided`

_The Run Nubbin tucks the shells under one arm and gives you a long, grateful look._  
**Warden Ollery**: Well, that’s that settled. Clop away, little one.  
_It trots a few steps to show you. Clip-clop, clip-clop. Two beats, over and over, steady as a clock._  
**Warden Ollery**: That’s a trot, that is. Real horses have a different rhythm for every speed.  
_The Run Nubbin tries walking instead. Clop, clop, clop, clop. Then something faster: ba-da-dum, ba-da-dum._  
**Warden Ollery**: Ha! Now it’s cantering. Three beats. Listen.  

> **Lesson** (music, do): keeping a steady beat; rhythms in 2, 3 and 4  
> **Warden Ollery**: Clap along with it. A horse’s walk is four even beats: one, two, three, four.  
> **Warden Ollery**: A trot is two beats: clip-clop, clip-clop. A canter is three: ba-da-dum, ba-da-dum.  
> _Keep each one steady, like a clock. That steady pulse under the music is called the beat._  
> Check: `edu:clap:rhythm:walk-trot-canter`
> _For grown-ups: Clapped three horse rhythms: a walk in four beats, a trot in two and a canter in three._

_It skids to a halt, very pleased with itself, and clops once more for applause._  

#### `q04-complete`

_The Run Nubbin, whose name turns out to be Trotwell, clops a lap of the whole Grove. Soon every Nubbin wants a go._  
**Warden Ollery**: I’ll be honest. I quite like the noise. It’s company.  
_As thanks, Trotwell teaches you the trot. It is mostly knees._  
_From now on, when you run, you can swap your footsteps for coconut hooves._  
_Far away on the beach, Gullwick sleeps soundly, wings spread out like a dropped coat._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): rest and sleep help bodies recover  
> _Gullwick has earned that sleep. After hard work, muscles need rest to recover and grow stronger._  
> _Sleep is when a lot of that repair happens. Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours a night._  
> _Gullwick is aiming for about 14. Nobody is going to argue._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that muscles recover during rest and sleep, and that children their age need about 9 to 12 hours a night._

_Beside it someone has left a fruit and a note in chalk: “Thank you for the noise. From the wall.”_  

### Glossary

- **vibrate**: To shake very quickly back and forth. Vibrations make sound.
- **headwind**: A wind blowing straight towards you as you travel, pushing against you.
- **compromise**: An agreement where each side gives up a little so both get something.
- **rhythm**: A pattern of long and short sounds and beats that repeats.
- **company**: Having someone or something with you, so you don’t feel alone.

## Q5. The Rabbit at the Ledge

- `q05-s1`: Ask Sparks to build something that can win over the rabbit. · _Sparks is in the Workshop. Bring one sun fruit; Sparks will need it._
- `q05-s2`: Take the Hand Melon to the ledge, count to exactly three, and toss it. · _Tap Count once per beat and throw on three. Too many or too few and it fizzles; Sparks will make another._

#### `q05-intro`

_On the cliff ledge above the falls, a crowd of Nubbins has gathered round something small, white and fluffy._  
_It is a rabbit. It is the size of a slipper. It is chewing a clover with total calm._  
**Sir Rollo Brisket**: Stand back, Keeper. My Nubbins and I have trained for this all week.  
_This is Sir Rollo Brisket, a Keeper with a cape, a cardboard crown and a great deal of confidence._  
_His strongest Power Nubbin creeps up behind the rabbit for a friendly karate bout._  
_There is a white blur. The Power Nubbin is suddenly sitting in a bush some way off, puzzled but fine._  
_The next Nubbin creeps up from the side. Blur. Bush. The next. Blur. Same bush. It is getting crowded._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): prey animals’ eyes see almost all the way round  
> _Rabbits are prey animals. The Nubbins crept up from behind, then from the side. The rabbit saw them every time. How?_  
> - ✅ Its eyes are on the sides of its head. → Yes. A rabbit’s eyes sit high on the sides of its head, so it can see almost all the way round. Rabbits are prey: animals that other animals hunt. Seeing danger early keeps them safe.
> - It has eyes in the back of its head. → Close! Not in the back, but on the sides. That lets it see nearly all the way round without turning. Rabbits are prey animals, so spotting danger early is how they stay safe.
> - It was just lucky. → Lucky every time? Look at its face: the eyes are on the sides of its head, not the front. That gives it a view almost all the way round. Very handy for a prey animal.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a rabbit’s eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it sees nearly all round and is hard to sneak up on._

**Sir Rollo Brisket**: Retreat! Everybody back! Back to the bottom of the hill!  
_Everyone runs about ten steps, then stops, because the rabbit has gone back to its clover._  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin try.**
    - Your Nubbin steps up bravely. Blur. Bush. It climbs out with a leaf on its head, giggling.
- **Watch the rabbit for a bit.**
    - You notice it never starts a fight. It only finishes them, very quickly, and then has a snack.

#### `q05-sparks`

**Sparks**: A rabbit beat ALL of them? One go each? Oh, I love that rabbit.  
**You**: We don’t want to beat it, though. Not really.  
**Sparks**: No? Then what DO we want? Every good invention starts with that question.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-2-ETS1-1, ask): engineering: define the problem first  
> **Sparks**: Engineers always start by saying what the problem really is. So, Keeper: what’s ours?  
> - ✅ Make friends with the rabbit, so nobody ends up in a bush. → Yes! That’s the real problem. We don’t need to win. We need the rabbit to like us. Now I know what to build. Something a rabbit would love.
> - Beat the rabbit at karate. → Hmm. Ten Nubbins tried that. The bush is full. Maybe the real problem is different: we want the rabbit to be friendly. Let’s solve that one.
> - Build a bigger bush. → Ha! That does solve a problem. Just not the right one. The real problem is that the rabbit doesn’t trust us. Let’s fix that instead.
> _For grown-ups: Practised the first step of engineering: saying clearly what problem you are trying to solve._

**Sparks**: Right. Leave it with me. One sun fruit, some ribbon, and a very small amount of fizz.  
_There is a crackle, a small blue flash, and a smell of toasted fruit._  
_Sparks comes out of the smoke with frizzy eyebrows and an enormous grin. “Nearly there!”_  

#### `q05-melon`

**Sparks**: Behold. The Hand Melon.  
_It is a sun fruit with a ribbon round it and a little paper tag. It hums faintly._  
**You**: It’s not a melon.  
**Sparks**: Melon sounds braver. Read the tag. The tag is important. I wrote it in my best voice.  
_You turn the tag over. The handwriting is very fancy and slightly singed._  
_It says: “Count up to three, and stop. On three, and only on three, let go.”_  
**Sparks**: Not two, which is lazy. Not four, which is showing off. Three. Then toss it, gently, near the rabbit. Not at it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.C.3, ask): odd and even numbers  
> **Sparks**: Two and four are both even. Three is the odd one out. But what makes a number odd?  
> - ✅ You can’t split it into two equal groups. → Exactly! Share 4 sun fruits between 2 Nubbins: 2 each, fair. Share 3: someone gets the extra one. That leftover one makes 3 odd. 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are all odd. That’s why I like them. They’re a bit wild.
> - It’s strange-looking. → Ha! Three is a bit curly. But odd has a maths meaning. An odd number can’t be split into two equal groups. Share 3 fruits between 2: one is always left over.
> - It’s bigger than 2. → Four is bigger than 2 too, and 4 is even. So that can’t be it. Odd means it won’t split into two equal groups. Three fruits, two Nubbins: one left over. Odd!
> _For grown-ups: Sorted 2, 3 and 4 into odd and even, and explained that odd numbers can’t be split into two equal groups._

**Sparks**: It goes off like a party. Nobody gets hurt. The rabbit loves parties. Probably.  

**Choices**

- **Practise counting first.**
    - **You**: One. Two. Three.
    - **Sparks**: Perfect. Do exactly that, but with feeling.
- **What if I count to four?**
    - **Sparks**: Then it just sits there, disappointed in you. So will I.
- **Let Sir Rollo do the honours.**
    - **Sir Rollo Brisket**: Allow me. One… two… a good few!
    - **Sparks**: THREE, Rollo.
    - The Hand Melon gives a small, sad fizz in his hand. Sparks takes it back and makes another without a word.

#### `q05-pop`

_One. Two. Three. You toss the Hand Melon in a gentle arc._  
_It bursts into a shower of fruit confetti: little sweet scraps of every colour._  
_The scraps drift down slowly, swaying, like snow. The hard little stalk drops straight down. Plop._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity and air resistance  
> _Gravity pulls everything down. So why does the confetti float, while the stalk drops like a stone?_  
> - ✅ The air pushes against the wide, light scraps. → Yes. Falling things push through air, and air pushes back. That push is called air resistance. A wide, light scrap gets a big push for its weight, so it drifts. A small, heavy stalk barely notices.
> - Confetti doesn’t have gravity. → It does! Everything is pulled down by gravity. That’s why the confetti lands in the end. But air pushes back against wide, light things. That’s air resistance, and it slows the confetti down.
> - Sparks made it magic. → Sparks would love that. But it’s air resistance: air pushing back on anything falling through it. Wide, light things like confetti get slowed a lot. Small, heavy things like the stalk hardly at all.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why light, flat confetti falls slowly: gravity pulls everything down, but air pushes up against wide, light things._

_The rabbit sits up, ears tall. It has never seen anything so wonderful in its life._  
_Its ears turn, one forward, one back, catching every tiny pitter and patter._
